item.title: Morning Edition, Thursday, November 26, 2026
item.description:
The Thanksgiving nor'easter left more than 250,000 U.S. homes and businesses without power early Thursday as it pushed up the East Coast, CNN reported. North Carolina and Virginia had nearly 130,000 customers out combined, with gusts up to 45 mph, and Missouri more than 78,000 as heavy, wet snow fell, according to PowerOutage.us. Gusts up to 70 mph are possible near the coast. FlightAware showed 328 U.S. flights canceled early Thursday after more than 6,000 were delayed Wednesday. New York City is under a high wind warning from 10 a.m. Thursday to 1 a.m. Friday, with gusts up to 65 mph expected, and the East Coast could see its highest water levels since Superstorm Sandy in 2012. The Macy's parade moves to Saturday at 8:30 a.m.; Philadelphia's parade was canceled and replaced with a TV event. In California, king tides and waves tore down part of a pier in Pacifica.

China said Thursday it reserves the right to take "necessary measures" against the new U.S. tariff plan, and Japan called its proposed 15% rate regrettable. Commerce Ministry spokesman He Yadong called the U.S. "overcapacity" finding a "pretext for protectionism" and urged Washington to "correct its erroneous practices" and return to dialogue. The U.S. trade representative on Wednesday proposed tariffs on 14 economies, including 20% on China, in line with a trade truce that expires in January; Jamieson Greer told CNBC the rate fits China's understanding and that about $30 billion of Chinese goods would be exempt. Japan's chief cabinet secretary, Minoru Kihara, said Japan has no structural excess production capacity. The EU has said it expects the U.S. to honor their deal's 15% ceiling. European stocks rose about 1.6% Thursday as investors judged the plan milder than feared, Reuters reported.

Congo's Ebola outbreak, the fastest-growing on record, has passed 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting disrupts the response. Nearly half of the 12,021 confirmed patients have died, Congo's Health Ministry data show, making it the deadliest of the country's 17 outbreaks. The outbreak, declared in May, is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved vaccine or treatment. Fighting between the army and CRP rebels resumed Thursday near Bunia, the response hub, and the WHO said clashes this week kept teams from some communities.

Every U.S. child will get two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from him, Elon Musk pledged Wednesday, a gift Axios values at about $18 billion. Musk doubled an Oct. 19 promise of one share per child next year. With about 72 million U.S. minors and SpaceX's Wednesday closing price, the gift would be worth about $18.35 billion, roughly triple Michael Dell's gift to the Trump accounts for children. SpaceX shares have fallen about 13% since the first pledge. Musk gave no timing for the distribution.

Nvidia's AA credit rating was put on watch for a possible downgrade by S&P Global Ratings, which cited weak board oversight and no credible succession plan. S&P said in a Wednesday note that news about the CEO and questions over possible export-control violations exposed weaknesses in Nvidia's board structure and effectiveness, and that the long tenure of some directors may compromise their independence. Any cut would likely be one notch, to AA-, within about 90 days, unless investigations show wider harm. S&P plans to meet the board and management. Moody's lowered its Nvidia outlook to stable on Nov. 18. Nvidia shares closed down 3.9% at $149.30 Wednesday.

Inflation rose to 3.8% in October by the Fed's preferred gauge, nearly double its 2% goal, the Commerce Department said Wednesday. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 0.3% from September and 3.8% from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September. Core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 3.3% from a year ago. Personal income jumped 0.7% and spending rose 0.3%; the saving rate was 4.1%. A separate Commerce report revised third-quarter growth up to a 4.3% annual rate, the fastest in three years. Markets fully price a quarter-point Fed rate hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting. Jobless claims fell to 189,000, near the lowest since the late 1960s.

U.S. stocks recovered most of a steep early drop Wednesday, with the S&P 500 closing down 0.3% after falling as much as 3.2%, AP reported. The Dow rose 164 points, or 0.3%, after falling more than 1,000 points early, and the Nasdaq slipped 0.6% after being down as much as 4.6%. AI stocks fell for a second day after Monday's Huang rally, as hot inflation data and new tariff proposals weighed early; Nvidia fell about 5%. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.85%, and Brent crude rose 3.5% to $94.61. The S&P 500 is down about 5.5% for November. Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and close at 1 p.m. Friday.

Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed to Saturday because of the coming nor'easter, as New Jersey declared a statewide emergency, AP reported. Macy's moved its 100th parade to Saturday, Nov. 28, at 8:30 a.m. after consulting city and agency partners, with gusts forecast to exceed balloon safety limits Thursday. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency in all 21 counties from 6 p.m. Wednesday, citing gusts of 50 to 70 mph, 1 to 4 inches of rain and moderate to major coastal flooding through Friday; the order does not restrict travel. The National Weather Service has high wind warnings for 17 New Jersey counties and coastal flood warnings for 12.

President Trump's second birthright-citizenship order was blocked Wednesday by a federal judge in Washington for a nationwide class of affected children. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper certified a class of children "who are or will be unlawfully denied citizenship" under the August order and granted a classwide preliminary injunction in Nathan v. Trump, brought by the ACLU and other groups. The order sought to deny citizenship to some U.S.-born children of foreign government or international-organization employees without diplomatic immunity, children born through commercial surrogacy, and children with a parent suspected of gang or terrorist membership. "The President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship," Cooper wrote in a 67-page opinion, noting the Supreme Court struck down the first order in June. He also denied the government's request for a stay pending appeal. A Maryland judge blocked the order for a separate class in September. The White House called it a ruling from "an activist judge."

Benjamin Netanyahu's trial judges told Israel's attorney general Wednesday that a bribery conviction in the main case against him is unlikely and urged a rethink. At an unusual Jerusalem District Court hearing, Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman said the chances of conviction in Case 4000, on bribery, fraud and breach of trust, "are low — to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter." The judges indicated Case 2000 may not involve a crime, leaving Case 1000, over gifts from Arnon Milchan and James Packer, as the realistic remaining charge, and suggested a quick wrap-up. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said prosecutors would consider the recommendations; no charges have been dropped. Netanyahu, indicted in 2020, denies all charges.

FinCEN, the Treasury's financial-crimes unit, took some systems offline after an intruder reached part of its network, an agency official said Wednesday. The official said Treasury is working with the FBI, CISA and outside forensic examiners to find the scope of the incident, and there is no evidence so far of a breach of the Bank Secrecy Act or beneficial-ownership databases. FinCEN gave filers relief: reports due Nov. 18 through Dec. 29 can be filed by Dec. 30. It follows this month's string of federal system problems, including a breach of an unclassified CIA and ODNI analysis system and a brief NSA network outage.

New tariffs of up to 35% on goods from China, the EU, Japan, India and 10 other economies were proposed Wednesday by the U.S. trade representative. USTR Jamieson Greer found that 14 economies' industrial policies create "structural excess capacity" that burdens U.S. commerce under Section 301. Proposed rates, on top of existing duties, include up to 20% for China, 15% for the EU, up to 15% for Japan and Taiwan, up to 25% for India, up to 18% for Thailand and up to 35% for Vietnam, with some goods exempt. Mexico and Norway were investigated but not covered. Comments are due Jan. 5, 2027, with hearings starting Jan. 25, so no new tariffs take effect before then. The duties would partly replace emergency tariffs the Supreme Court struck down in February.

1Password, the password manager, said Wednesday an attacker reached some backend systems and copied customer names and sign-in emails; vaults were not affected. The company said vault data and the keys protecting it were safe, it contained the intrusion, restored clean services and rotated internal credentials. Customers do not need to change anything but should watch for phishing emails posing as 1Password invitations or account-recovery requests.

item.title: Morning Edition, Wednesday, November 25, 2026
item.description:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia left the United States for Spain Tuesday night, ending a 20-month fight over his deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said. Reuters reported that DHS said he "has self-deported" to Spain, while his lawyers said he left "on his terms." The Washington Post, citing two people briefed, said the departure was part of a negotiated agreement between his attorneys and government lawyers; its terms have not been made public. His flight left just after 10 p.m. Eastern from Dulles after a mechanical delay, and officials removed his ankle GPS monitor beforehand. Abrego Garcia, 31, was wrongly sent to a Salvadoran prison in March 2025 despite a court order, and returned in June 2025 after a Supreme Court order that the government facilitate his return. The administration had sought to deport him to African countries; he had asked to go to Costa Rica. Sen. Chris Van Hollen said the deal respects his will and his due process rights.

A fast-strengthening coastal storm will bring strong wind, heavy rain and coastal flooding to the East Coast Wednesday and Thanksgiving Day, the National Weather Service says. The Weather Prediction Center said low pressure off the Southeast coast will intensify and track north. Coastal flooding is the biggest concern Wednesday and Thursday, from Georgia and the Carolinas to the Northeast, with high tides and onshore winds. Rain of 1 to 4 inches is forecast for the Carolinas and Mid-Atlantic and 1 to 2 inches for southern New England. Gusts of 50 mph or more are likely along the coast, with 45 mph or more inland to the I-95 corridor, and power outages and tree damage are possible. High Wind Warnings cover parts of New Jersey, Maryland's Eastern Shore, Delaware and Pennsylvania. A Slight Risk of excessive rainfall covers the Carolina coast Wednesday and the northern Mid-Atlantic Thursday.

South Africa's Western Cape High Court on Wednesday set aside the Phala Phala panel report that had revived impeachment proceedings against President Cyril Ramaphosa. The court said the independent panel "fundamentally misconstrued its functions" and made errors of law, and declared invalid all proceedings arising from the report, which effectively ends Parliament's impeachment process for now, Daily Maverick reported. Opposition parties including the ATM, EFF and MK party are expected to appeal. The report concerned the theft of $580,000 from Ramaphosa's farm in 2020; the Constitutional Court revived the process in May 2026. Full reasons for the ruling have not been released, and Speaker Thoko Didiza said she would study it.

South Korea's stock index fell 6.16% Wednesday to 4,697.51, dropping below 5,000 as the AI trade stumbled again, Yonhap reported. Trading was briefly halted when the Korea Exchange triggered a five-minute sell-side sidecar on program buying, which applies when KOSPI 200 futures drop at least 5%. Samsung Electronics lost 9.87% and SK hynix 11.05%. Yonhap tied the drop to Tuesday's U.S. tech selloff, when Nvidia gave back part of its previous-day jump and concerns over new U.S. tariffs weighed on tech shares. The index had rallied the day before.

Huawei, the Chinese telecom giant, was convicted Tuesday of deceiving banks about its business in Iran and stealing trade secrets from U.S. companies. A federal jury in Brooklyn found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice, but acquitted it of racketeering conspiracy. Prosecutors said Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its Iran dealings and stole technology over two decades, including Cisco router source code. The trial ran more than two months with over 60 prosecution witnesses. Huawei said the convictions lack legal merit and it will take "all necessary legal actions" to defend itself. The case began in 2018 with the arrest in Canada of CFO Meng Wanzhou, whose charges were later dropped under a deferred prosecution deal. Sentencing has not been set.

The Army's Iowa lead azide blast is set for 9 a.m. Central Wednesday, a FEMA alert said, warning some people within 5 miles they may be evacuated. The alert told people 5 to 20 miles from the Middletown plant to stay indoors with windows closed. FEMA said it is helping residents southwest of the site who choose to leave (1-800-621-3362), and the EPA said it will test homes, schools and properties for lead on request; USDA said about 350 farms could be in the plume's path. At a Tuesday news conference, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said a controlled, mitigated blast is "far preferable" to an accidental one; officials said crews added sand barriers, water and gel blocks, and that snow and a sharp temperature drop forecast for Wednesday make the 68 barrels less stable. The Army's last lead azide detonation this large was in 1977. Gov. Kim Reynolds now supports the plan after talking with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Telle said the Army will examine every storage site nationwide.

Consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 in November, its highest level since January 2025, the Conference Board said Tuesday. The index rose 11.4 points from an upwardly revised 91.9 in October, far above the roughly 92 economists expected. The present-situation index rose 13.7 points to 132.8 and the expectations index 9.9 points to 83.6. The share of people saying jobs are "plentiful" rose to 30.8% and "hard to get" fell to 18.4%. Twelve-month inflation expectations eased for a second month to 5.7%. The board's economist said the gain may reflect "lower uncertainty following the midterm elections"; confidence rose sharply among Democrats and independents and dipped slightly among Republicans. Consumers still voiced frustration with high prices. Survey period: Nov. 1-17.

China's anti-corruption agency is investigating Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the ruling Politburo, state news agency Xinhua said Tuesday. Xinhua said Chen is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws," a phrase that usually means corruption. Reuters reported he is the fourth member of the Politburo to be investigated since 2025, after He Weidong, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui. Chen, 62, a former Tsinghua University president, environmental protection minister and Beijing mayor, had been seen as a possible contender for higher office. Analysts quoted by Reuters said the announcement was a surprise.

New U.S. strikes on Iran may come after the New Year if talks fail, President Trump told Fox News; Iran's top negotiator said Tuesday it will not talk until its conditions are met. In comments to Fox News on Sunday, Trump said he is inclined to order strikes after the new year without a deal, called Iran's negotiators "professional tap dancers" and said Iran is "more aggressive now than before the election." He dared Iran to challenge the U.S. naval blockade of its ports. On Tuesday, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's lead negotiator, told parliament Iran will not negotiate with the United States until its "seven conditions" are met, state-affiliated Mehr News Agency reported. Iran has demanded an end to the blockade, sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets before formal talks.

Nvidia fell about 7% Tuesday, giving back part of Monday's jump, as chip stocks pulled the Nasdaq down 1.5% while the Dow rose. The Nasdaq Composite lost 1.49% to 23,730.37 and the S&P 500 slipped 0.49% to 7,201.98, while the Dow gained 0.85% to 50,016.49, Reuters reported. Investors weighed governance and political questions about Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO and braced for possible new tariffs. Other chip stocks such as Micron and AMD also slid, and Anthropic shares fell below their $83 IPO price. Health care and consumer staples gained.

A CIA computer system that handles open-source intelligence was breached in a cyberattack, a person familiar with it told the AP on Tuesday. The person, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said no classified information was involved and the issue has been resolved. It is not clear who was responsible. The New York Times first reported the breach, saying some unclassified information of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence was also exposed. The CIA has not commented publicly.

USSF-266, a classified Space Force mission, launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, Tuesday morning. Liftoff was at 8:08 a.m. PT (11:08 a.m. ET) from Space Launch Complex 4E after several schedule slips. The first-stage booster, on its 29th flight, landed on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific. Payload details were not released.

Oilfields in Kurdish-controlled parts of four Iraqi provinces will be run by Baghdad's Oil Ministry, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered Tuesday; Kurdish leaders objected. The order covers fields in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh under Kurdish security control, puts all Kurdistan border crossings under the federal crossings authority, closes unofficial crossings and requires oil exports to go only through the federal Oil Ministry, after an oil-smuggling inquiry. Al-Zaidi also removed the head of the border crossings authority and suspended North Oil Company's director general. KDP leader Masoud Barzani called the move "troubling" and said anti-smuggling steps must follow legal and constitutional channels.

Riyadh's tallest skyscraper, home of Saudi Arabia's wealth fund, was hit by the Houthis for the second time in a week, wounding 11 people. Saudi Civil Defense said the injured were two Saudis, four Egyptians, three Nepalis and two Indians. The Saudi-led coalition called it a "cowardly terrorist attack" on a tower in the King Abdullah Financial District; the 385-meter PIF tower was also struck Nov. 19 without injuries. Yemen's Houthis have targeted Saudi airports, oil sites and office towers since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, a spillover of the U.S.-Iran war. Separately, local officials said an airstrike on buses and trucks in Lahj province killed 26 people, and Britain sanctioned the Houthis and four leaders.

item.title: Morning Edition, Tuesday, November 24, 2026
item.description:
The Army will blow up nearly five tons of unstable explosive in Iowa on Wednesday morning, it said, after a federal appeals court cleared the plan Monday night. A three-judge 8th Circuit panel denied the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club's emergency request to keep the EPA's permit on hold, saying the groups were unlikely to win and that the degraded lead azide risks "an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion" without the permit's safeguards; the underlying challenge continues. Earlier Monday, President Trump said the detonation of 68 drums at the Middletown plant would wait for the court and be "fully subject" to Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing. Sand did not say yes or no, saying the administration "should make this decision" on the information from its own experts and urging it to share that information with the public. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said every agency involved agreed the Army should proceed with a "carefully controlled detonation" Wednesday morning, and the Army said Gov. Kim Reynolds supports it.

New U.S. strikes on Iran may come after the New Year if talks fail, President Trump told Fox News; Iran's top negotiator said Tuesday it will not talk until its conditions are met. In comments to Fox News on Sunday, Trump said he is inclined to order strikes after the new year without a deal, called Iran's negotiators "professional tap dancers" and said Iran is "more aggressive now than before the election." He dared Iran to challenge the U.S. naval blockade of its ports. On Tuesday, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's lead negotiator, told parliament Iran will not negotiate with the United States until its "seven conditions" are met, state-affiliated Mehr News Agency reported. Iran has demanded an end to the blockade, sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets before formal talks.

Rep. Ilhan Omar could claim the privacy protections of a sitting member of Congress during the federal search of her home, unsealed court records show. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh, who approved the Oct. 12 search of the Minnesota Democrat's Washington home, rejected the Justice Department's view that the Speech or Debate Clause privilege covers only official offices and some devices; the government agreed to a protocol letting Omar assert the privilege before agents searched. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the partial unsealing after more than a dozen news organizations sued, but kept the 67-page search warrant affidavit sealed. The heavily redacted filings shed no new light on why the search happened or what it found. Omar has not been charged and denies wrongdoing; the AP has reported investigators are examining her family's immigration paperwork.

A car bomb outside the Meta state governor's office in Villavicencio, Colombia, wounded 21 people Monday night, local health officials said. Meta's health department said 21 people were hurt, including five security guards at the building; police reported no deaths. The blast heavily damaged the government building on the city's central park and nearby buildings. President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed "narcoterrorism" and said his government will not negotiate with armed groups; no group has claimed the attack.

An explosion at a crowded hot pot restaurant in Hanoi, Vietnam, killed six people and injured more than a dozen Tuesday morning, local time. Police said preliminary findings point to a gas explosion that brought down part of the building; more than 14 people were hospitalized, one with a traumatic brain injury, and rescuers searched the rubble for anyone trapped. Nearby houses were damaged and residents of unsafe buildings were moved.

Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO and president Monday, effective immediately, less than two weeks after he resigned; the company's shares jumped about 31%. Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring Huang back, and to his board seat, after meetings in which it said it was satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead." The board said it received input from "senior levels of the United States government" and is confident his return "poses no national security risk." Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. officials suspected of working for Chinese intelligence; board chair Harvey Jones said on the Nov. 17 earnings call that the board did not intend to reinstate him. President Trump called it "the correct and proper decision" on Truth Social and said the attorney general has no evidence Huang broke the law. Colette Kress, interim CEO since Nov. 12, returns to her finance role. Nvidia closed up about 31.5%, its best day since 2000, adding roughly $900 billion in market value.

The S&P 500 jumped 4.7% Monday, its best day since April 2025, as Huang's return to Nvidia ended a seven-day slide in U.S. stocks. The S&P 500 closed at 7,237.17, the Nasdaq Composite rose 6.5% to 24,089.56 and the Dow gained about 1,448 points, or 3%, to 49,595.31, recovering more than half of last week's plunge that pushed the S&P and Dow into a correction. Chip stocks led: the Philadelphia semiconductor index rose 14%, with Micron up 19% and TSMC up 15%. Nasdaq 100 futures rose so fast before the open that a rare circuit breaker was triggered, Bloomberg reported. The VIX fear gauge fell about 25%. Separately, New York Fed President John Williams said Monday the Fed has "work to do" on inflation and must act "over time" to reach its 2% goal; markets fully price a quarter-point rate increase at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.

The Army's planned detonation of nearly five tons of unstable explosive in Iowa is on hold after President Trump ordered it paused Monday until a court allows it. Trump said the military will not blow up the 68 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown until the 8th Circuit lets it proceed, and made it "fully subject" to Iowa Governor-elect Rob Sand agreeing. He said a controlled blast would be safer and that he would hold Sand responsible for any harm if the material is not destroyed. The Army had planned the detonation for Wednesday despite the court's pause of the EPA emergency permit, and the Justice Department asked judges Sunday to lift that pause. Environmental groups sued over health and pollution risks to nearby residents.

NATO is sending an AWACS early-warning aircraft to Poland after three Russian cruise missiles crashed there Friday, alliance and Polish officials said Monday. Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski announced the deployment after an emergency North Atlantic Council meeting in Brussels; a NATO spokesperson said the alliance's top commander, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, authorized it and is examining additional assets. Poland asked allies for stronger air defenses on the eastern flank but did not invoke Article 4. Polish prosecutors say all three objects were Kh-101 missiles; Zalewski called the incursion an "obvious provocation."

Grok, Elon Musk's AI chatbot, let users make sexualized images of real people, including children, without consent, Virginia and Oregon charged in lawsuits Monday. Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones sued SpaceX, which now runs X and xAI, saying the companies failed to stop Grok from generating non-consensual intimate images and child sexual abuse material while promoting the platform as safe; Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed a separate, similar suit. The states seek penalties and new consumer protections. Virginia says Grok could fabricate sexual images from a single existing photo.

Chip stocks led: the Philadelphia semiconductor index rose 14%, with Micron up 19% and TSMC up 15%. Nasdaq 100 futures rose so fast before the open that a rare circuit breaker was triggered, Bloomberg reported. The VIX fear gauge fell about 25%. The Army's planned detonation of nearly five tons of unstable explosive in Iowa is on hold after President Trump ordered it paused Monday until a court allows it. Trump said the military will not blow up the 68 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown until the 8th Circuit lets it proceed, and made it "fully subject" to Iowa Governor-elect Rob Sand agreeing. NATO is sending an AWACS early-warning aircraft to Poland after three Russian cruise missiles crashed there Friday, alliance and Polish officials said Monday. Grok, Elon Musk's AI chatbot, let users make sexualized images of real people, including children, without consent, Virginia and Oregon charged in lawsuits Monday. Judge Toby Heytens wrote the opinion, joined by Judge DeAndrea Benjamin; Judge Robert King concurred in part and dissented in part. A federal judge blocked Connecticut's similar mask law on Nov. 20.

Social media companies cannot be held liable for the 2022 Buffalo supermarket massacre, New York's highest court ruled Monday, 4-3. The Court of Appeals upheld dismissal of suits by survivors and victims' families against YouTube, Reddit, Twitch, Discord, 4chan and others, which argued the platforms radicalized the white supremacist gunman who killed 10 Black people at a Tops market. The majority said the shooter's conduct was so extraordinary that it was not a foreseeable result of the platforms' design, so the companies were not the legal cause of the injuries.

item.title: Morning Edition, Monday, November 23, 2026
item.description:
A powerful Thanksgiving storm is expected to bring heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding to the East Coast Wednesday and Thursday, the National Weather Service says. The Weather Prediction Center said Monday that "confidence is high for an impactful holiday storm" from Wednesday through Saturday. The heaviest rain is expected on Thanksgiving Day along the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast coasts: 1 to 4 inches in the Carolinas and Mid-Atlantic and 1 to 2 inches in the Northeast, with a risk of flooding rain from the Virginia Tidewater to southern New England. Gusts of 50+ mph are forecast along the coast and 40+ mph inland along the I-95 corridor, with power outages and downed trees possible. High surf and high tides could bring significant coastal flooding and beach erosion from Georgia to the Northeast, and snow showers are possible Friday into Saturday. Forecasters urged travelers to monitor forecasts.

The death toll from Sunday's Russian drone strike on an apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, rose to 11, regional officials said Monday. Kyiv regional military administration head Tymur Tkachenko said rescuers recovered another body from the rubble; Sunday evening's count was four. Emergency crews worked through the night, pausing only for air-raid alerts, and pulled a 7-year-old boy alive after 14 hours under the debris, the State Emergency Service said. Three more people were killed Sunday when a drone hit a supermarket in Vyshneve.

Russia's corvette Merkury, one of its newest warships, was sunk by Ukrainian sea drones at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Monday. Zelenskiy said seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were used near the Libyan coast and also hit a second target, the Russian cargo ship MV Angara, which he said Russia used to carry weapons; a Russian Ka-27 helicopter was destroyed with the corvette, which entered service in 2023. "We continue operations in designated waters," he said on Telegram. Libya's eastern government reported an explosion and fire on a Russian ship at the Benghazi naval base early Sunday and opened a joint investigation with Russia. Russia had not commented.

The Army plans to blow up nearly five tons of unstable explosive material at an Iowa ammunition plant Wednesday despite a court pause, and the Justice Department asked judges Sunday to lift it. A federal appeals court on Thursday paused an EPA permit for destroying nearly 70 drums of lead azide, a compound used to set off munitions, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, after environmental groups sued over a possible lead-dust plume over Iowa, the Mississippi River and parts of Illinois. In a filing late Saturday the Justice Department said the order does not stop the Army from acting under a separate legal authority, arguing the material could explode on its own as temperatures drop. The Army moved the detonation to Wednesday for better weather; Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the state emergency operations center and the FAA restricted flights over the area through Wednesday.

U.S. stock futures jumped Monday after last week's AI-driven rout, while South Korea, Taiwan and China moved to steady their own sliding markets. Nasdaq 100 futures rose 3.3% and S&P 500 futures 2.5% by 3:51 a.m. ET, Reuters reported, after the Nasdaq's 10% drop last week, its worst since March 2020. South Korea's KOSPI, now half its peak, still fell about 3.3% as the finance minister repeated plans to stabilize the market if needed; Taiwan's regulator tightened short-selling rules and Taiwan stocks rose 2.1%; Chinese exchanges eased margin-financing rules. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.96% and gold gained 2.1%. Dell reports Tuesday.

House Democrats reached at least 258 seats Sunday, their largest majority since 1992, after Rep. Virginia Foxx conceded her North Carolina race following a recount. Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a longtime local newspaper journalist, defeated Foxx, the 11-term chair of the House Rules Committee, by about 330 votes out of roughly 287,000 cast in North Carolina's 5th District; the AP called the race Sunday afternoon after the recount. The 258 seats top the 257 Democrats won in 2008 and match their 1992 total; a few races are still uncalled. With the Senate also in Democratic hands, Hakeem Jeffries is on track to become the first Black House speaker in January, facing a Republican president who has vowed to veto Democratic bills.

All three objects that crashed in Poland on Friday were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles, Polish prosecutors said Sunday, not two missiles and a drone as first reported. The Lublin regional prosecutor's office said wreckage at Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Mołodycz in southeastern Poland all came from Kh-101s, which preliminary findings show were built in the fourth quarter of 2026 in Dubna, near Moscow; lab tests are not finished. Work at Mołodycz resumes Monday. NATO's North Atlantic Council meets in Brussels Monday to discuss the incursions. No one was hurt; Russia has not commented.

The UN's COP31 climate talks in Turkey collapsed Sunday without a final agreement after the European Union and others rejected a deal that did not mention fossil fuels. Summit president Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, told the closing session in Antalya that the main decisions were not adopted for lack of consensus. Ireland's climate minister, speaking for the EU, said the bloc would not endorse an "Antalya Pact" that does not even mention fossil fuels; an earlier draft had called for a faster phase-out before later versions dropped the language. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was "deeply disappointed." The summit ran two days past its scheduled end, the longest UN climate conference on record.

Delta Air Lines flights were delayed nationwide Sunday after its weight-and-balance computer system failed, forcing an FAA ground stop at Atlanta days before Thanksgiving. The FAA said the problem was with Delta's automated system for calculating aircraft weight and balance, not air traffic control; it issued a ground stop and then a ground delay at Hartsfield-Jackson at Delta's request. Delta used manual workarounds and said Sunday afternoon the system was working again. About 1,650 Delta flights, roughly half the day's schedule, were delayed by 4 p.m. ET, about 70% of them from the outage, but only a few dozen were canceled. Separately, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Sunday Americans should expect more technology outages as companies and agencies replace aging systems.

Yemen's Houthis said Sunday they attacked Saudi Arabia's Rabigh oil refinery on the Red Sea coast; Saudi authorities did not immediately comment. Rabigh, about 165 km north of Jeddah, is home to Petro Rabigh, a refining and petrochemical complex built by Saudi Aramco and Japan's Sumitomo Chemical. The Houthis have claimed several attacks on Saudi energy sites in recent months; Saudi Arabia has not confirmed hits on any refinery. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy claimed two unnamed supertankers hit mines and stopped near the Strait of Hormuz; the claim has not been independently confirmed.

Nvidia must explain its chip sales to China and who handled compliance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday on CBS's "Face the Nation." Bessent said the administration has been in touch with Nvidia's interim management, lead directors and lawyers: "We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there... Did it go all the way to the top?" Asked about President Trump's call for ousted CEO Jensen Huang to apologize and return, Bessent said, "we have to see where the buck stops." Nvidia's board chairman has said the board will not rehire Huang, who resigned after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy.

item.title: Morning Edition, Sunday, November 22, 2026
item.description:
Bahrain said an Iranian attack late Saturday hit a civilian industrial facility and set it on fire; no one was hurt. Bahrain's Interior Ministry did not name the site; residents told AFP they saw smoke over Sitra Island, home to state oil company Bapco's refinery. The Bahrain Defence Force said air defenses intercepted several Iranian attacks and that falling shrapnel caused damage but no casualties. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they fired missiles and drones at U.S. positions at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in retaliation for U.S. drone flights over Iran, and claimed two Patriot radars were hit; U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond. Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet and has reported several Iranian attacks this week after a lull of several weeks.

A Russian drone collapsed much of a five-story apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, early Sunday; at least 14 people may be trapped, Zelenskyy said. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said the strike destroyed apartments from the ground to the upper floors; rescuers evacuated nine people, including a child, and a teenager was hospitalized with shrapnel wounds. Kyiv regional chief Tymur Tkachenko said the blast also damaged a kindergarten and a shop. The search of the rubble was continuing.

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, the cartel boss called "El Chapo Isidro" and one of the FBI's 10 most wanted, was captured in Mexico, officials confirmed Saturday. Mexico's security chief said Saturday morning that army and National Guard special forces captured Meza Flores and two other leaders of his organization Friday night in Guasave, Sinaloa, in an operation the defense ministry said was coordinated with U.S. intelligence. He was flown to Mexico City to face prosecutors; Mexico says he faces a U.S. extradition order on drug-trafficking charges. The U.S. offered up to $5 million for him and says his group smuggled heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana into the United States for more than 20 years. The raid set off firefights and burning roadblocks across northern Sinaloa; Mexico's Defense Cabinet said Saturday afternoon that seven suspected cartel gunmen and four soldiers were killed.

U.S. Central Command denied Saturday an Iranian claim that Iran's air defenses hit a U.S. F-16 over the Gulf and forced it to make an emergency landing. Iranian state media said air defenses targeted the jet Friday evening, causing it to abort its mission and land at a nearby airport. "Iran did not attack a US F-16 fighter aircraft yesterday — at all," Central Command said, adding that all U.S. fighter jets in the Middle East were safe and accounted for. Iran has made similar claims during the war that the U.S. military has denied.

Polish prosecutors confirmed Saturday that a missile that crashed in Poland was a Russian Kh-101 built this year, as NATO's chief vowed to defend "every inch" of Polish territory. Investigators in Lublin said propulsion and guidance parts recovered at Nowy Lipowiec, about 60 km from the Ukrainian border, came from a Russian-made missile manufactured in the fourth quarter of 2026; work continues at the other two crash sites. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte met Prime Minister Donald Tusk in Warsaw, called the incursion "clearly dangerous" and said NATO commanders are assessing deterrence and defense. Poland has asked for more NATO support on the eastern flank but has not invoked Article 4 consultations. No one was hurt; Russia has not commented.

A Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad, the Sparta II, caught fire after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland Saturday; Finland's military said Ukraine was likely behind it. Finland's coast guard was alerted at about 8:50 a.m. local time (1:50 a.m. ET), about 50 km west of Suursaari island; the burning ship drifted into Finnish waters and its crew was evacuated to a Russian vessel. Kaliningrad's governor said two drones were used. The ship, run by a company tied to Russia's defense ministry, is under U.S. and Ukrainian sanctions. Finland set temporary air and sea restrictions and said a Russian helicopter may have violated its airspace. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said "war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity." Kyiv has not commented. No environmental damage was found.

Two more tankers leaving the Strait of Hormuz were hit by unidentified projectiles off Oman early Saturday, less than an hour apart, the British navy's UKMTO center said. The first tanker was struck on its stern about 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at about 0500 GMT (midnight ET); about 50 minutes later a second outbound tanker was hit in its engine room about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab. No one was reported hurt, and any environmental damage was not yet known, UKMTO said. The attacks follow Friday's strike that set a tanker on fire about 8 nautical miles north of Khasab. The ships were not named.

Brazil's former President Jair Bolsonaro was moved to intensive care Saturday with an intestinal obstruction while serving a 27-year prison sentence. He is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his 2022 election loss.

item.title: Morning Edition, Saturday, November 21, 2026
item.description:
The FBI's national crime database, which police use to check warrants and run background checks, was apparently breached by hackers, CNN reported Friday night. The FBI is investigating the suspected intrusion into the National Crime Information Center, which federal, state and local agencies use to share warrants, criminal histories and background-check data, according to two people briefed on the probe, CNN reported; Reuters and NBC News carried the report. The FBI did not comment. It would be the second breach of an FBI system in recent months, after a September hack of an FBI jobs website exposed data on employees. Separately, NBC News reported that a U.S. Department of Agriculture system used to pay farmers was hit by a cyberattack this week; USDA has not commented publicly.

Two more tankers leaving the Strait of Hormuz were hit by unidentified projectiles off Oman early Saturday, less than an hour apart, the British navy's UKMTO center said. The first tanker was struck on its stern about 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at about 0500 GMT (midnight ET); about 50 minutes later a second outbound tanker was hit in its engine room about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab. No one was reported hurt, and any environmental damage was not yet known, UKMTO said. The attacks follow Friday's strike that set a tanker on fire about 8 nautical miles north of Khasab. The ships were not named.

The Trump administration's overhaul of a $4 billion homelessness program was unlawful, a federal judge ruled Friday, blocking a shift of money away from permanent housing. U.S. District Judge Mary McElroy in Providence, R.I., ruled in a suit by 22 states, the District of Columbia and housing groups that the Department of Housing and Urban Development broke the McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act by adding grant criteria for the Continuum of Care program, including a plan to set aside $1.3 billion for transitional housing and services-only grants. She also struck limits on needle-exchange work and a "self-sufficiency" test. HUD must let applicants revise applications until Dec. 1 and award the money by Dec. 31. HUD Secretary Scott Turner said the ruling disrupts funding days before awards and that HUD may appeal. An appeals court had overturned her earlier order on different grounds.

The S&P 500 and the Dow both fell into a correction Friday, more than 10% below their record highs, as the AI stock sell-off deepened. By preliminary closing figures, the S&P 500 fell 3.59% to 6,918.45, its seventh straight loss and longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq dropped 5.13% to 22,654.15 and turned negative for 2026, and the Dow lost 1.85% to 48,188.18. All three had their worst week since April 2025. Nvidia fell about 14% and Micron about 14%; Anthropic's shares posted a steep loss on their second day of trading. Bitcoin dropped below $60,000. Traders are pricing a near-certain quarter-point Fed rate hike in December.

An Anthropic mathematician, Levent Alpöge, says he and the company's Claude AI found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, math's most famous unsolved problem; experts have not confirmed it. Alpöge posted the proof in the Lean language, which checks each step by computer, and said it covers the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland told Scientific American he compiled the Lean code independently and called it "an historic moment," but said much work remains to understand the proof. The 1859 problem, about the pattern of prime numbers, carries a $1 million Clay Mathematics Institute prize.

A tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz caught fire Friday after being hit by an unknown projectile, the British navy's UKMTO center said; no one was hurt. The strike happened about 8 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at 1500 GMT. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the tanker hit a mine. It is at least the third tanker reported hit near Khasab since Monday. Separately, the Treasury Department sanctioned four Iranian regime insiders it said sell oil for the government, including a former Revolutionary Guards intelligence officer.

Russia fired more than 400 drones and about 110 missiles at Ukraine overnight, killing at least eight people, after Putin vowed revenge for strikes on the Crimea bridge. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said 27 of the missiles were ballistic and that the attack targeted energy, railway and logistics sites. Six people died in Kyiv, three of them water-utility workers, and two at a railway station in Lviv. Three bridges over the Dnipro in Kyiv were hit, and emergency power cuts hit western Ukraine. Ukraine's air force said it downed 380 drones, 79 cruise missiles and three ballistic missiles.

Two Russian missiles and a drone crashed in Poland during Friday's barrage on Ukraine, and NATO's chief visits Warsaw Saturday; Poland called it a deliberate provocation. Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said a Kh-101 cruise missile fell near Nowy Lipowiec, a second object believed to be a missile near Rudnik nad Sanem and a jet-powered drone near Mołodycz, all in southeastern Poland. No one was hurt. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the objects were certainly Russian and the timing, during a British- and French-led Coalition of the Willing drill in Poland, looked intentional. Poland will ask NATO for more support on its eastern flank; NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte called the incident "clearly dangerous." Russia has not commented.

item.title: Morning Edition, Friday, November 20, 2026
item.description:
A sweeping bill to speed up federal permits for power lines, pipelines, mines and wind and solar farms passed the Senate Thursday night and now goes to the House. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (H.R. 2347 as amended) passed 62-33. Fifteen members of the Democratic caucus voted yes along with nearly all Republicans; 31 Democrats and Republican Sens. Josh Hawley and Mike Rounds voted no, many Democrats citing weaker environmental protections. The bill shortens reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act and Clean Water Act, gives federal regulators new authority over interstate transmission lines, and aims to keep power customers from paying for grid hookups to data centers. President Trump backs the deal; the House is expected to take it up after Thanksgiving.

Stock markets fell around the world Friday as the AI sell-off deepened, putting Asian shares on track for their worst week since March 2020. Japan's Nikkei fell 5%, and Taiwan's market was down 17% for the week, its biggest weekly drop since 1990. MSCI's index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan is down 8% this week. Europe's STOXX 600 fell 1.5% and Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.5%; MSCI's world index fell for a seventh straight session, its longest losing streak since 2023. Investors bought bonds, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield below 5%. Anthropic's record IPO Thursday did not restore confidence in AI spending, analysts told Reuters.

The White House national cyber director, Sean Cairncross, was fired after a week of outages hit air travel, banks and the NSA, a person close to the White House said. The source said the president "fully supported" the firing; Defense Department chief information officer Kirsten Davies takes the job temporarily. Cairncross, confirmed in August 2025, said it was the "honor of a lifetime" to serve. The top U.S. intelligence official said Wednesday the outages were separate maintenance and technical failures, not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack. A permanent successor needs Senate confirmation; Democrats take control of the Senate in January.

Florida executed Thomas Overton for the 1991 murders of a Florida Keys couple, the state's 20th execution this year, a record. Overton, 71, was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. at Florida State Prison after the U.S. Supreme Court denied a stay; his last words were "I never killed anyone." He was convicted of raping and killing Missy MacIvor, who was eight months pregnant, and killing her husband, Michael. Florida executed 19 people in 2025; two more executions are scheduled in December. Later Thursday, Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes, 70, in a procedure that took over an hour as staff struggled to find a vein, AP reported.

Baseball's career hits leader Pete Rose was posthumously pardoned by President Trump for his 1990 tax crimes. Trump announced the "Complete and Total Pardon" on social media Thursday. Rose, who died in 2024 with 4,256 hits, pleaded guilty in 1990 to filing false tax returns, months after accepting a lifetime ban from baseball over betting. Major League Baseball reinstated him last year.

Anthropic's stock closed its first trading day about 17% above its $83 IPO price, but the wider market fell about 2% as AI shares slid. Anthropic opened at $111.50 shortly before noon, briefly valuing the company above $2 trillion and topping $115, before fading to close near $97. The S&P 500 erased an early 1.3% gain and fell about 2% for a sixth straight loss, its longest losing streak since April 2024; the Dow fell about 1,100 points (2.2%) to back below 50,000 and the Nasdaq lost about 2.3%. AMD dropped about 10% after investigative outlet Hunterbrook disclosed a short position citing its China dealings; AMD denied wrongdoing.

Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, the U.N.'s top court ruled Thursday, the first time it has found a country itself responsible for genocide. The International Court of Justice found that Myanmar's security forces intentionally killed Rohingya, caused them serious bodily or mental harm and imposed measures meant to prevent births during the 2017 "clearance operations" in northern Rakhine state, and that Myanmar failed to prevent and punish genocide. The court cited an estimated 10,000 Rohingya killed; about 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. It ordered Myanmar to investigate and prosecute those responsible, allow safe return of displaced Rohingya, and compensate them, with the amount to be set later; Myanmar must report back within two years. The judgment in the case brought by The Gambia in 2019 is final, binding and without appeal. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres welcomed it.

A resolution directing President Trump to pull U.S. forces out of the Iran war failed in the Senate, 48-51, in Congress's first war vote since the midterms. Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Rand Paul voted for the House-passed measure (H.Con.Res. 93); Democrat John Fetterman voted against it, and Republican Thom Tillis, who backed an earlier attempt, also voted no. As a concurrent resolution it would not have gone to the president. Democrats say they will keep pushing war-powers votes and use spending bills to end the war once they control Congress in January. The Pentagon lists 23 U.S. service members killed in the conflict.

Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine after the war, U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said after talks with European leaders in Berlin. Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and dozens of European leaders; Trump called into the meeting after his talks with Xi and Putin in China. Kushner said an Article 5-style U.S. guarantee is "a really, really big deal" that Trump is open to if it serves U.S. interests, and that Russia agreed to talks that include Europe. No date is set for the next round. Putin, speaking in Shenzhen, vowed to respond to Ukraine's strikes on the Kerch Bridge and said he would not be negotiating ceasefires.

The Comanchero motorcycle gang and Italy's 'Ndrangheta mafia were sanctioned by the Treasury Department Thursday for helping drug cartels move cocaine and launder money. OFAC said the Australia-based Comancheros worked with the Sinaloa Cartel, CJNG and other cartels on multi-hundred-kilogram cocaine shipments, and named 'Ndrangheta leaders and funeral-home and limousine businesses in Ontario, Canada. The action was coordinated with police in Australia, New Zealand, Italy and Canada. In a separate action the same day, Treasury sanctioned cyber-scam operators in Cambodia and facilitators tied to an armed group in Myanmar's Karen State.

Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration was withdrawn by President Trump the night before a key Senate committee vote, citing too little support. A White House official said the nomination lacked enough support in Congress; the Senate health committee, where Republicans hold a one-seat edge, was due to vote Wednesday. Committee chair Bill Cassidy said the White House "abandoned a viable confirmation path." Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy aide, faced criticism over her views on vaccines and abortion. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas is being weighed as a replacement, sources told Reuters. The FDA has had no Senate-confirmed leader since Marty Makary left in May. (Missed in our Nov. 18-19 editions.)

A Homeland Security rule capping how long foreign students, exchange visitors and foreign journalists can stay in the U.S. was struck down by a federal judge in Boston Monday. U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor vacated the July rule nationwide, finding it "arbitrary and capricious" and beyond DHS's authority. It would have replaced open-ended "duration of status" admission for F, J and I visa holders with fixed stays of up to four years, required many to apply for extensions, and limited some PhD, joint-degree and program changes. "DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity... that Congress sought to permit and encourage," Saylor wrote. The rule never took effect after he blocked it in September; the government's appeal of that order is pending. (Missed in our Nov. 16-17 editions.)

The NSA's classified internal network was still down Thursday, a third day, with some staff told to work from home, NBC News reported. Two sources told NBC the outage, which began during maintenance Tuesday, has not affected intelligence collection and shows no sign of a cyberattack. It also hit an NSA site in Georgia that handles Middle East work.

JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard said outside vendors were hit by a cyberattack that exposed some customers' names and email addresses, but no card numbers. A ransomware group leaked marketing data including about 16,000 email addresses tied to JPMorgan's invitation-only Reserve program, Cybernews reported. JPMorgan said its own systems and services were not disrupted, it will offer affected customers free credit monitoring, and the breach has no connection to its outage earlier this week. Visa said there is no sign card numbers were affected; Mastercard said a limited number of emails from one benefit program were exposed.

Weekly applications for unemployment benefits rose by 1,000 to 203,000, still low by historical standards, the Labor Department said. Initial claims for the week ending Nov. 14 were 203,000, seasonally adjusted; the four-week average rose 2,000 to 197,750. Continuing claims rose 70,000 to 1.763 million in the week ending Nov. 7, with the insured unemployment rate unchanged at 1.1%.

item.title: Morning Edition, Thursday, November 19, 2026
item.description:
Trump, Xi and Putin issued a joint "peace declaration" after their first three-way meeting, pledging U.N. reform and that nuclear war "must never be fought," with no arms-control deal. The leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers met for about 90 minutes in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday local time (Wednesday evening ET) on the sidelines of the APEC summit, after Trump held separate meetings with Xi and Putin. The four-point declaration, posted by the White House, says the three will reform the U.N., increase production and supply of refined petroleum products, respect the immunity of state officials (saying the International Criminal Court and similar bodies "must not abuse their jurisdiction"), and hold a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the spread of nuclear weapons. It sets no limits on any country's arsenal. Putin did not commit to attending the G20 summit in Miami next month, Reuters reported. Trump then left China for Washington.

Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, the U.N.'s top court ruled Thursday, the first time it has found a country itself responsible for genocide. The International Court of Justice found that Myanmar's security forces intentionally killed Rohingya, caused them serious bodily or mental harm and imposed measures meant to prevent births during the 2017 "clearance operations" in northern Rakhine state, and that Myanmar failed to prevent and punish genocide. The court cited an estimated 10,000 Rohingya killed; about 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. It ordered Myanmar to investigate and prosecute those responsible, allow safe return of displaced Rohingya, and compensate them, with the amount to be set later; Myanmar must report back within two years. The judgment in the case brought by The Gambia in 2019 is final, binding and without appeal. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres welcomed it.

President Trump said the U.S. will "see what happens" with Iran after Jan. 1, a day after warning "we'll wipe them out" if Iran set off a dirty bomb in Washington. Trump did not explain the significance of Jan. 1 in the interview broadcast Thursday, Reuters reported. On Wednesday, asked about a reported Iranian dirty-bomb plot, he said residents of Washington need not panic but that the U.S. would "wipe them out" if it happened, and said there was an indication Iran was "looking at" gases and biological weapons, without giving evidence. Trump has alternated between threatening escalation and suggesting he could wind down the nine-month war. Israel has passed intelligence to the U.S. on Iran's military buildup, officials told Reuters.

Denmark's parliament unanimously approved the U.S.-Denmark-Greenland security pact Thursday, opening the way to a bigger U.S. military role in Greenland. The vote was 109-0, U.S. Ambassador Ken Howery said. The deal, signed in September by Trump and the Danish and Greenlandic prime ministers and already approved by Greenland's parliament, updates a 1951 defense agreement to give the U.S. underwater access and permission to build a missile-defense system, and says Greenland would stay in NATO if it became independent. Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the last step before it takes effect is a U.S. notification to Congress, and that the U.S. has not yet told Denmark of plans for new bases. Trump had threatened earlier this year to take control of the island.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, raising about $81 billion in the largest stock offering ever and valuing the AI company near $1.5 trillion. The maker of the Claude AI models sold 980 million shares, above its planned $70-$78 range and more than the 825 million first offered, AP reported; the proceeds top SpaceX's roughly $75 billion IPO in June. Shares begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Anthropic said it had $33.24 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, and a net loss of $104 billion, most of it from accounting changes on convertible notes and other instruments, CNBC reported.

Almost all Fed officials expect more interest-rate increases will likely be needed, minutes of their October meeting showed. At the Oct. 27-28 meeting, 10 members voted to hold the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4%; Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Almost all participants judged that further increases would likely be appropriate to bring inflation back to 2%, and a couple said a hike larger than a quarter point could be considered at the Dec. 8-9 meeting if inflation data were unfavorable. Almost all also discussed the risk that returns on AI investment disappoint investors. The S&P 500 fell for a fifth straight day Wednesday, its longest losing streak since June, and the Dow dropped 561 points, AP reported.

The U.S. and Venezuela signed a deal restoring military ties for the first time in 21 years, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in Caracas. Hegseth, the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit since U.S. forces captured Nicolás Maduro on Jan. 3, met acting President Delcy Rodríguez. He said the agreement covers joint training, intelligence sharing, equipment and efforts to strengthen Venezuela's military, and cooperation against criminal and terrorist groups. Officials did not say whether it allows U.S. bases or permanent troop deployments, and its full terms were not released. Hugo Chávez cut defense ties with Washington in 2005.

Flooding from more than 15 inches of rain swamped parts of South Florida, collapsing a synagogue roof and closing schools in Broward and Miami-Dade. Hollywood, Sunrise and Plantation in Broward County got more than 15 inches over 72 hours. The roof of Temple Sinai in Hollywood collapsed early Wednesday; no one was hurt. State wildlife officers rescued more than 70 residents from a flooded Hollywood apartment complex, and I-95 ramps and Florida's Turnpike flooded. Broward and Miami-Dade public schools were closed Thursday, and a flood watch with 2 to 4 more inches possible ran through Thursday evening, CBS Miami reported.

item.title: Morning Edition, Tuesday, November 17, 2026
item.description:
Online banking at Chase and other big U.S. banks was back to normal early Tuesday; Chase blamed a software bug in its own hardware, not a cyberattack. Downdetector showed service back to normal at the banks and Zelle early Tuesday, CBS News reported. JPMorgan Chase told Reuters on Monday it had "a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" with no evidence it was cyber-related, and that other banks were affected only when they were party to a transaction with Chase: "This is not a systemic issue." Chase had nearly 4,800 Downdetector reports by 2 p.m. ET Monday. Separately, United Airlines said Monday evening it had resolved a widespread system outage that delayed departing flights.

The Crimean bridge was hit by Ukraine for a second straight day, halting traffic, and two people were killed in the attack on Crimea, its Russian-installed governor said. Sergei Aksyonov said traffic across the 12-mile road and rail bridge was suspended. Unverified video appeared to show the bridge's road arch span collapsed into the Kerch Strait; Reuters could not verify it, and there was no official word on the extent of damage. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy confirmed the attack, calling it a response to Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure. Russia's Defense Ministry said it shot down 1,441 Ukrainian drones over 22 regions, a record for the war. Russian strikes overnight hit Kyiv's bridges and caused power outages in eight Ukrainian regions. The Kremlin said Putin was informed ahead of his trip to China for a three-way summit with President Trump and Xi Jinping.

Bahrain's air defenses intercepted Iranian drone attacks early Tuesday, the third in five days; Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed they targeted a U.S. radar. Blasts were heard over Manama after Bahrain's Interior Ministry sent a "possible threat" alert, later followed by an all-clear; state television said the armed forces intercepted "Iranian aerial attacks." The Revolutionary Guards said their drones targeted a U.S.-operated radar at Sheikh Isa Air Base in response to U.S. drone flights over Iran; no damage has been confirmed. U.S. Central Command had not commented. After Friday's attack, CENTCOM said it shot down two Iranian drones with no damage or injuries.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Middle East, giving the U.S. three aircraft carriers in the region, U.S. Central Command said Monday. The Roosevelt and its strike group, which left San Diego in September, join the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, there to keep up the naval blockade of Iranian shipping. The flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, with two more destroyers in the Red Sea, the Navy said. President Trump has alternated between threatening new large-scale strikes on Iran and saying the war is "militarily effectively over."

Online banking at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and other big U.S. banks failed for thousands of customers Monday; Chase blamed a technical issue, not a cyberattack. Customers began reporting trouble Monday morning, and by 2 p.m. ET nearly 4,800 users had reported problems with Chase on Downdetector, the most of any bank, including balances, transfers, wires and check deposits. Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo, Truist and Capital One customers also reported problems. "Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," Chase said. U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly hit but Zelle transfers with other banks could be delayed; Capital One said it was operating normally; Zelle said its network was working and that a problem at Chase may be delaying payments. A Justice Department official told MS NOW there was no evidence of an attack. No full restoration had been announced by publish time.

A new Commerce Department rule bars China and other restricted countries from reaching advanced U.S. AI chips remotely through data centers abroad. The Bureau of Industry and Security issued the interim final rule Monday, saying it was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council. Companies now need licenses to export, reexport or transfer advanced AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere that may provide computing power to companies based in China, Russia, Iran, North Korea or other embargoed (D:5) countries, including through brokers; it covers sites above about 12 million TPP, roughly 750 Nvidia H100-class chips. It also adds license requirements for advanced chip shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, except to U.S.-based companies, gives existing data-center operators 90 days to get licenses, and formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. It comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO.

Federal agency officials must now get White House approval before testifying to or briefing Congress, under a memo from White House Counsel William Scharf. The Nov. 16 memo directs all executive agencies to clear congressional testimony and briefings with the White House Counsel's office and the Office of Legislative Affairs in advance. Axios first reported the memo; PBS NewsHour published its full text.

The Supreme Court turned away the Trump administration's bid to revive canceled University of California research grants, and a challenge to Maryland's limits on guns in sensitive places. In Monday's order list, the justices declined the administration's appeal of a 9th Circuit ruling that canceling about $150 million in NSF and NEH grants to UC researchers over diversity-related work likely violated the First Amendment; the grants keep flowing while the case continues in district court. The Court also refused to hear gun-rights groups' challenge to Maryland's bans on carrying guns in places such as schools, parks, public transit, hospitals, bars and government buildings, leaving in place a 4th Circuit ruling upholding them; Justice Clarence Thomas wrote that he is skeptical of such laws and would take up a narrower case. The Court separately ended Custodia Bank's bid to force the Federal Reserve to give it a master account.
