U.S. stocks had their worst day in more than a week Monday, with the Nasdaq down 2.5% and the Dow off 737 points, as Nvidia slid before earnings. The S&P 500 fell about 1.9%; chipmakers led the drop as the AI-chip sell-off that hit Asia on Monday spread to Wall Street, while defensive stocks such as Procter & Gamble and McDonald's rose. Nvidia reports quarterly results Tuesday.

A suspect was arrested Monday in the explosive device found at a Peoria, Ill., ethanol plant, a law enforcement official told CNN; the FBI has not confirmed it. Peoria Mayor Rita Ali said plant leadership told her a suspect is in custody and that the FBI, which leads the case, will release more. The official said others who may have been involved are still under investigation and there is no suspected foreign-terrorism link. Peoria police retracted an earlier statement about a person in custody; the FBI confirmed only "law enforcement activity" and said any charges would appear in federal court records. No motive has been released. Friday's find at BioUrja Renewables forced a roughly day-long evacuation of a one-mile area including downtown Peoria.

Dozens of Bahraini Shiite clerics were sentenced to life in prison on charges of forming a terrorist group tied to Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Bahrain's prosecutor said. The rights group BIRD says 64 people, most of them clerics, got life terms, 13 of them in absentia, and five got 15 years. The verdicts come as Iran has targeted Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, with drone attacks in recent days.

item.title: Morning Edition, Monday, November 16, 2026
item.description:
A tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz caught fire in its engine room after an unknown projectile hit it, Britain's maritime security agency said. UKMTO said the ship's company security officer reported the strike as the tanker headed out through the strait early Monday local time (Sunday evening ET); no one was hurt and all crew were accounted for. It is a separate incident from Sunday's attack on an eastbound tanker. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said, via state media, that an oil tanker hit naval mines east of the strait and caught fire, but named no ship and gave no images; that claim has not been independently confirmed. ABC News, citing a U.S. official, reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group has entered the Central Command area, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. CENTCOM had not commented on the Iranian claims.

Asian stock markets fell Monday, with Taiwan down 6% and South Korea 3.6%, as the AI chip sell-off after Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit spread. TSMC fell 5.7%, SK Hynix 7.9% and Samsung Electronics 4.5%. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 2.4%. U.S. stock futures were lower ahead of Nvidia's earnings Tuesday. Brent crude rose 0.6% to $96.40. Separately, Japan's Cabinet Office said real GDP fell 0.02% in July–September from the prior quarter (0.1% annualized), its first contraction in four quarters, as private consumption fell 0.3%.

International student enrollment at U.S. colleges fell 9% this fall, and new foreign students dropped 15%, a survey released Monday found. The Institute of International Education surveyed more than 800 colleges. Graduate enrollment of international students fell 15% and undergraduate 3%, with fewer students from India. Participation in the OPT post-graduation work program fell 6%. Of colleges surveyed, 88% cited visa processing and 70% travel restrictions. NAFSA estimated the decline cut foreign students' contribution to the U.S. economy by $2.4 billion.

Huge waves flooded California beaches for a second day Sunday, closing piers from Ventura to San Diego and prompting an evacuation warning near Capitola. The National Weather Service warned of surf up to 35 feet in the Bay Area, plus rip currents and sneaker waves; waves above 50 feet were recorded Saturday in San Mateo County. Piers in Ventura, Manhattan Beach, Huntington Beach and Pacific Beach closed, and water flooded beachfront homes in Seal Beach. Large surf is expected all week.

The Crimean bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea was hit by Ukraine overnight, halting traffic until about midday, its Russian-installed governor said. Sergei Aksyonov said traffic would be restricted; damage appeared minor and no casualties were reported. Traffic stopped at about 2:22 a.m. Moscow time (6:22 p.m. ET Sunday), and four passenger trains were delayed. Russia's Defense Ministry said Ukraine launched 1,336 drones overnight; Moscow's mayor said about 600 headed toward the capital.

Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia on Dec. 1 after a foiled arson attack on a drone maker it blames on Russian military intelligence. Eight people were detained over the attempted overnight arson at defense firm Threod Systems; no one was hurt. Estonian security services said the GRU ordered it. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said closing the three crossings would reduce the threat and signal that attacks on Estonia's defense industry are unacceptable; he did not say when they would reopen. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said he expects new EU sanctions on Russian individuals and entities at a meeting in Brussels on Monday. Russia's Foreign Ministry called the move "Russophobia."

A tanker was attacked in the Gulf just before entering the Strait of Hormuz Sunday, Britain's maritime security agency said; its crew is safe. UKMTO said Indian shipping authorities reported the attack on the eastbound tanker and that the damage and any environmental harm were not yet known. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers using an "unauthorised route" in the southern strait hit naval mines and that one, a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude, sank; they named neither ship. That claim has not been independently confirmed, and UKMTO said it was unclear whether its report was the same incident. The U.S. military recently said it had cleared mines from the strait's main routes, and the U.S. had not commented on Sunday's claims.

The FAA ground-stop investigation is focused on two newly installed routers in Arkansas and Texas, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday. Duffy said on Sunday news shows that a router switched on during a copper-to-fiber upgrade in El Dorado, Ark., and one installed about three weeks ago in Amarillo, Texas, flooded the air traffic network with data; both are being examined at contractor L3Harris's lab in Florida with the FBI's help. He said the broadcast function has been turned off on all 69 routers of that type and that there is no sign of a hack or sabotage, but the root cause is not yet known. President Trump, in his first comments on Friday's 4 1/2-hour halt, posted that Congress must approve the money for a new air traffic control system "FAST." Duffy says the $12.5 billion Congress gave the FAA last year cannot pay for new telecom networks; House Transportation Democrats said most of that money is still unspent. The FAA expected flight schedules to be back to normal by the end of Sunday.

Drones struck three commercial ships near Romania's Sulina canal late Saturday, two inside Romanian waters, and Romania scrambled fighter jets, its government said. Defense Minister Stefan Radu Oprea said the Greek-flagged tanker Evia Petrol V, the bulk carrier Marsol and the tanker Ali Najafov were hit; crews put out fires and no one was hurt. A fourth ship was hit Friday. Prime Minister Luca Niculescu called the strikes unacceptable and a violation of international law but did not say who launched the drones; Russia denies targeting Ukraine's neighbors. The canal links the Danube to the Black Sea and carries Ukrainian exports. Romania is asking NATO allies for more patrols and counter-drone gear.

Bahrain's military said it shot down several Iranian aerial attacks Sunday, as Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed they hit a U.S. base there. It was the first time since September that Bahraini air defenses had to intercept attacks; the Interior Ministry twice warned residents to take shelter. The Guards said they launched six drones at a U.S. air-defense radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for "hostile U.S. actions," Iranian state media reported. There was no immediate comment from the U.S. military. Two days earlier the U.S. denied an Iranian claim of hitting a radar in Bahrain, saying it intercepted two drones without damage. Separately, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces said they were pulling back from the area overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, leaving the Houthis in control of it.

item.title: Evening Edition, Sunday, November 15, 2026
item.description:
The FAA ground-stop investigation is focused on two newly installed routers in Arkansas and Texas, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday. Duffy said on Sunday news shows that a router switched on during a copper-to-fiber upgrade in El Dorado, Ark., and one installed about three weeks ago in Amarillo, Texas, flooded the air traffic network with data; both are being examined at contractor L3Harris's lab in Florida with the FBI's help. He said the broadcast function has been turned off on all 69 routers of that type and that there is no sign of a hack or sabotage, but the root cause is not yet known. President Trump, in his first comments on Friday's 4 1/2-hour halt, posted that Congress must approve the money for a new air traffic control system "FAST." Duffy says the $12.5 billion Congress gave the FAA last year cannot pay for new telecom networks; House Transportation Democrats said most of that money is still unspent. The FAA expected flight schedules to be back to normal by the end of Sunday.

Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia on Dec. 1 after a foiled arson attack on a drone maker it blames on Russian military intelligence. Eight people were detained over the attempted overnight arson at defense firm Threod Systems; no one was hurt. Estonian security services said the GRU ordered it. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said closing the three crossings would reduce the threat and signal that attacks on Estonia's defense industry are unacceptable; he did not say when they would reopen. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said he expects new EU sanctions on Russian individuals and entities at a meeting in Brussels on Monday. Russia's Foreign Ministry called the move "Russophobia."

A tanker was attacked in the Gulf just before entering the Strait of Hormuz Sunday, Britain's maritime security agency said; its crew is safe. UKMTO said Indian shipping authorities reported the attack on the eastbound tanker and that the damage and any environmental harm were not yet known. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers using an "unauthorised route" in the southern strait hit naval mines and that one, a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude, sank; they named neither ship. That claim has not been independently confirmed, and UKMTO said it was unclear whether its report was the same incident. The U.S. military recently said it had cleared mines from the strait's main routes, and the U.S. had not commented on Sunday's claims.

Rory McIlroy won the European tour's season-long Race to Dubai title for a record-tying eighth time Sunday; Tyrrell Hatton won the final event. McIlroy shot a bogey-free 67 to finish second at the DP World Tour Championship, holding off Spain's Eugenio Chacarra by about 125 points in the standings. He ties Colin Montgomerie's record and has won the title five years in a row. Hatton won the tournament by five strokes at 15 under. McIlroy dedicated the title to his father, who has been hospitalized for two months.

Drones struck three commercial ships near Romania's Sulina canal late Saturday, two inside Romanian waters, and Romania scrambled fighter jets, its government said. Defense Minister Stefan Radu Oprea said the Greek-flagged tanker Evia Petrol V, the bulk carrier Marsol and the tanker Ali Najafov were hit; crews put out fires and no one was hurt. A fourth ship was hit Friday. Prime Minister Luca Niculescu called the strikes unacceptable and a violation of international law but did not say who launched the drones; Russia denies targeting Ukraine's neighbors. The canal links the Danube to the Black Sea and carries Ukrainian exports. Romania is asking NATO allies for more patrols and counter-drone gear.

item.title: Morning Edition, Sunday, November 15, 2026
item.description:
Bahrain's military said it shot down several Iranian aerial attacks Sunday, as Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed they hit a U.S. base there. It was the first time since September that Bahraini air defenses had to intercept attacks; the Interior Ministry twice warned residents to take shelter. The Guards said they launched six drones at a U.S. air-defense radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for "hostile U.S. actions," Iranian state media reported. There was no immediate comment from the U.S. military. Two days earlier the U.S. denied an Iranian claim of hitting a radar in Bahrain, saying it intercepted two drones without damage. Separately, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces said they were pulling back from the area overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, leaving the Houthis in control of it.

A Copa Airlines jet and a UPS cargo plane collided while taxiing at Miami International Airport Saturday night, leaving two people with minor injuries. The FAA said the wingtip of the Copa Boeing 737, which had just landed from Panama City, struck the nose of the UPS Boeing 767 around 9:15 p.m.; controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight. All 166 passengers and six crew members got off the Copa plane. The two injured people were treated at the scene. The FAA is investigating. It came a day after the nationwide ground stop.

East Potomac Park and its public golf course in Washington can't be closed for now, a federal judge ruled Saturday, hours before Trump's planned shutdown. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order through Nov. 28 barring the government from closing the park and course during their usual hours; the course was due to close Sunday for a 15-month rebuild into a championship venue. She cited Trump's own social media posts on the closure date and said the government's reasons appeared to be after-the-fact justifications, but she did not order it to actively manage the park. The suit was brought by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers. Trump criticized the judge on social media Saturday.

The tanker's voyage data recorder from Friday's New Orleans cruise ship collision has been recovered, the NTSB said, with a preliminary report due within 30 days. The recorder captures the ship's speed, direction and course plus audio from the bridge. NTSB member John DeLeeuw said 16 investigators are on site for about a week and plan interviews; a final report is expected in 18 to 24 months. The cause of the Atlantic Asphalt's apparent steering loss is still unknown. Mayor Helena Moreno said it could take weeks to remove the sunken American Heritage.

SpaceX's Starship upper stage was caught by its launch tower's arms Saturday, the first time a ship returning from orbit has been recovered that way. Ship 42 came back to Starbase, Texas, after about 14 orbits and nearly a day in space on Flight 15, which lifted off Friday and released 26 Starlink V3 satellites. SpaceX confirmed the catch at about 3:21 p.m. CT. The other half of the planned double recovery failed Friday: the Super Heavy booster aborted its own tower catch and was sent to a splashdown in the Gulf. SpaceX had caught boosters on three earlier flights but had never tried to catch the ship.

Peoria's evacuation order was lifted Saturday after a search of the ethanol plant where a bomb was found turned up no other devices. Police Chief Brad Dixon ended the one-mile evacuation around Peoria's BioUrja Renewables plant at 1 p.m. CT, about a day after more than 5,000 people were told to leave; East Peoria's zone and the Illinois River also reopened. No arrests have been made, and officials would not discuss the device, suspects or a motive. The FBI and ATF are investigating.

Friday's nationwide flight halt began during contractor L3Harris's routine swap of old FAA phone lines to fiber, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. Duffy said the work at a remote FAA site flooded air traffic control routers with connection attempts; investigators are still checking whether it was installer error or a faulty router. L3Harris said it is cooperating. FAA chief Bryan Bedford said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or of an AI tool's role, expected 4,000 to 5,000 cancellations Saturday, and said airlines should be back on full schedules by Sunday night. Duffy raised his request to Congress for air traffic control upgrades to $50 billion.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said U.S. negotiators asked for the first time whether Ukraine would leave the Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership. In remarks released by his office Saturday, Zelensky said Ukraine will not give up land but that he would put a full package, with security guarantees, a strong army and rebuilding funds, to a national referendum if the U.S. and NATO partners confirm it. He rejected Russia's call to settle European security first and dismissed Putin's offer of a local truce in Kostiantynivka. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met him in Dublin on Thursday after talks with Putin.

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won Alaska's governor's race, the AP projected, the first Democrat elected to the office since 1998. The former state lawmaker defeated three Republicans, including Trump-endorsed Bernadette Wilson; AP called the race at 12:01 a.m. EST Saturday. He succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and was endorsed by Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski. His win means Democrats will hold 30 governorships. Alaska voters also rejected a ballot measure to repeal the state's open primaries and ranked-choice general elections.

PAHO plans to announce it Tuesday, Nov. 17. The CDC counted 5,412 confirmed cases this year through Nov. 12, more than double 2025's total, the most since the early 1990s. Bitcoin fell to about $65,000 Saturday, its lowest in three months, after losing about 13.5% over the past week. The largest cryptocurrency slid nearly 3% more after U.S. stock markets closed Friday. item.title: Morning Edition, Saturday, November 14, 2026
item.description:
The FAA's nationwide ground stop ended at 8:15 p.m. Friday after more than four hours, and officials blamed overloaded, decades-old network equipment. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said radar and communications at air traffic control centers began showing "instability" shortly after 3:30 p.m. ET, and the FAA halted departures nationwide at 3:54 p.m. "Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data ... and because of that, we shut the system down," he said at a White House briefing, blaming "an incredibly old air traffic control system" and asking Congress for billions to overhaul it. AP reported officials said new technology being added to the system overloaded the antiquated equipment, causing intermittent communications and radar gaps. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said nothing so far pointed to a cyberattack. It was the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years; more than 2,000 flights were canceled Saturday, and Duffy said operations should be back to normal by Thanksgiving travel.

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won Alaska's governor's race, the AP projected, the first Democrat elected to the office since 1998. The former state lawmaker defeated three Republicans, including Trump-endorsed Bernadette Wilson; AP called the race at 12:01 a.m. EST Saturday. He succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and was endorsed by Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski. His win means Democrats will hold 30 governorships. Alaska voters also rejected a ballot measure to repeal the state's open primaries and ranked-choice general elections.

A bomb found at an ethanol plant in Peoria, Ill., forced more than 5,000 people to evacuate, and the FBI is hunting whoever planted it. BioUrja Renewables, the former ADM plant, reported a bomb threat to police just after 1 p.m. CT Friday. Authorities judged a package there a credible threat, set a one-mile blast radius and evacuated more than 5,000 residents and workers in Peoria and East Peoria. Police Chief Brad Dixon said the device was "rendered safe" Friday night, but the evacuation order stayed in effect while the large facility is searched. "We're not considering this a hoax," he said. No arrests or injuries have been reported.

States can wait until July 1 to drop people from Medicaid for not meeting the new work requirement, the Trump administration said. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services told state Medicaid directors Friday that the requirement still starts Jan. 1 and states must still check whether enrollees and applicants are working, in school or volunteering, but they may choose not to remove anyone or deny coverage for failing it until July 1. CMS said states are making progress but face implementation challenges. Democrats taking control of Congress in January want to roll the requirement back.

President Trump will hold a three-way meeting with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen next week, the White House said. Spokeswoman Olivia Wales said Trump will end his China visit for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with the trilateral meeting and will discuss reducing nuclear weapons, among other topics; Iran may also come up. A senior U.S. official said no agreement is expected. Trump attends an ASEAN summit in the Philippines on Tuesday and meets Xi one-on-one Thursday. Moscow and Beijing had not confirmed the three-way talks. The last U.S.-Russia nuclear arms treaty expired in February.

All U.S. airports were ordered to stop departures Friday afternoon after a communications failure hit the FAA's air traffic control centers. The FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center ordered a national ground stop at 3:53 p.m. ET "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety," telling all departing traffic to stay on the ground until further notice; inbound international flights are handled case by case and planes already in the air may land. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communication issue was affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers and FAA technicians were investigating. No cause or restart time had been given as of about 4:45 p.m. ET. The last nationwide ground stop was in January 2023, when a pilot-notice system failed.

A river cruise ship with about 129 passengers rolled onto its side in New Orleans after a tanker struck it at the dock. The tanker Atlantic Asphalt hit American Cruise Lines' paddlewheeler American Heritage at about 12:30 p.m. CT Friday on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans administration building, about two hours after it docked to let passengers off, the port said. Rescuers pulled people from the water; the mayor's office said about a dozen people were taken to hospitals and search-and-rescue work was continuing. The cruise line said guests and crew were evacuated. The Coast Guard closed the river between mile markers 93 and 96. Officials have not confirmed the number of injuries or the cause.

Everyone aboard the New Orleans river cruise ship hit by a tanker was accounted for, with 32 people hospitalized and none critically hurt, officials said. Mayor Helena Moreno said 30 people from the American Heritage and two Harbor Police officers who joined the rescue were taken to hospitals, mostly with bumps and bruises; no one on the tanker was hurt. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said the tanker Atlantic Asphalt appeared to have had "some type of loss of steering" but the exact cause is not known. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating, with investigators sent by ground after Friday's flight halt. The Coast Guard ended the search and is working to reopen the river and salvage the capsized paddlewheeler.

Workday, the payroll and HR software used by thousands of employers, went down Friday, locking workers out of timecards, pay information and benefits enrollment. The Pleasanton, Calif., company said a problem found while testing its backup systems left some data in an inconsistent state, and it put some systems into maintenance mode while it works on a fix, promising updates every 30 minutes. It gave no time for full restoration. Workday says more than 11,500 organizations use it, including Walmart and Target, though it has said only some customers were affected. Separately, Microsoft said Saturday its Outlook and Teams services were fully restored after an outage that began Thursday.

Rep. Lauren Boebert lost her Colorado seat to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, the AP projected Friday. AP called Colorado's 4th District at 12:53 p.m. MT with Laubacher at 48.8% to Boebert's 47.9% and about 99% of votes counted. The district voted for President Trump by 18 points in 2024. Boebert has not conceded; she said earlier she would not run again in 2028 if she lost. Colorado's House delegation will be 7-1 Democratic.

U.S. Air Force personnel at Britain's RAF Lakenheath responded to suspected unauthorized drone activity Friday, and the base sheltered in place. An Air Force spokesperson said security forces responded Friday evening U.K. time and that no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected. The local member of Parliament said the incident was resolved with no threat to the public. On Monday the U.S. moved more than a dozen aircraft from nearby RAF Mildenhall over a reported Iran-linked threat.

Wisconsin reported a second child death in its measles outbreak as confirmed cases reached 651. The state health department reported the death of a child in Grant County; its outbreak page lists 651 confirmed cases as of Nov. 13, the state's highest count in about 35 years. Reuters also reported Pennsylvania's seventh measles-linked death.

The U.N. nuclear watchdog said it does not know the location or status of Iran's Isfahan enrichment plant and called that a serious proliferation concern. A confidential IAEA report to member states, seen by Reuters, said the agency does not know the plant's exact location or whether it contains nuclear material, and that the lack of access must be fixed "with the utmost urgency." Iran says normal inspections cannot resume until the "root causes" are addressed. Separately, Iran's Assembly of Experts called a review of the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty an "unavoidable necessity."

Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, and their 6.5% gain over the past year is the largest since 2022, the Labor Department said. The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3% after a revised 1.4% jump in September. Goods prices rose 0.5%, led by a 1.3% rise in food, while energy edged down 0.1%; services rose 0.2%. Over 12 months the index is up 6.5%, the most since November 2022. Prices excluding food, energy and trade services rose 0.5% for the month and 4.9% over the year. The Fed meets Dec. 8-9.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's department for not blacklisting chip buyer Megaspeed. On CNBC Friday, Bessent said Treasury, State, the Pentagon and the U.S. trade representative had favored putting Megaspeed on the export blacklist for months but that "Commerce has the pen," and said he was frustrated by advanced chips leaking to China. The dispute follows Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation on Thursday. Commerce had not commented.

item.title: Morning Edition, Friday, November 13, 2026
item.description:
Microsoft's Outlook and Teams outage ran into a second day Friday, with fixes failing and governments and companies worldwide still affected. The disruption began about 11:17 a.m. ET Thursday, according to Microsoft's service health dashboard, and more than 130,000 users reported problems that day. Microsoft said overnight its latest fixes were "not taking as expected" and that some restored servers became unresponsive again once traffic returned; it has given no time for full recovery. Exchange Online mail was hit hardest, with Exchange-dependent Teams calendar and scheduling features also failing. Officials in Singapore, Japan and Australia reported impacts, and Microsoft said there was no indication of malicious activity.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they struck a U.S. early-warning radar in Bahrain, their first claimed attack on a Gulf country since September. The Guards said the strike, reported by Iranian state media Friday, retaliated for what they called an air attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik in southern Hormozgan province, and called it a "serious warning" to the U.S. The Guards also said a liquefied petroleum gas tanker hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. Neither claim could be independently verified, and the U.S. and Bahrain, home of the Navy's 5th Fleet, had not commented. The claims come during a fragile lull in the war that began Feb. 28.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen said he will challenge Chuck Schumer to lead the new Democratic Senate majority, calling for "new leadership." The Maryland Democrat announced Thursday night that he will run for majority leader in a closed-door, secret-ballot caucus vote next month (Dec. 1, per CNN). "It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," he said. Schumer, Democratic leader since 2017, said he has "the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader." Van Hollen said he has more than 10 commitments and called himself the underdog; Sen. Bernie Sanders and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed back him, and Sen. Angus King backs Schumer. Democrats will hold at least 55 seats.

Democrat Cindy Holscher won the Kansas governor's race, AP projected Thursday, keeping the office in her party's hands. Holscher, a state senator, led Republican Ty Masterson, the Trump-endorsed state Senate president, 50.3% to 49.7% with 98% of votes counted when AP called the race at 5:43 p.m. ET, nine days after the election. It was the state's closest governor's race since 1974, and Kansas had never before elected back-to-back Democratic governors; she succeeds term-limited Gov. Laura Kelly. Masterson conceded in a statement. Democrats had already secured a majority of U.S. governorships for the first time in two decades.

The Brooklyn apartment building collapse killed eight people, including two children, New York's mayor said as the search for victims ended. The toll rose from two on Wednesday. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said two of the dead were construction workers and 18 people were hurt in the collapse and rescue. The three-story building on Flatbush Avenue gave way Wednesday afternoon while workers were digging at a neighboring lot; the cause is under investigation. The fire department ended rescue operations Thursday, and Mamdani ordered safety inspections at about 100 building sites tied to the companies involved in the construction project.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned effective immediately, and finance chief Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a successor. Nvidia's board said Thursday it accepted Huang's resignation as president, CEO and director; it will consider internal and external candidates. Kress, CFO since 2013, keeps that job while serving as interim CEO. Harvey C. Jones, a former Synopsys CEO on the board since 1993, was named Nvidia's first-ever board chair. The resignation follows Huang's admission Sunday of an affair with a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy, and a New York Times report of a second relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% Thursday before recovering about half of that loss, the Associated Press reported. Nvidia still plans to report quarterly results Tuesday, Nov. 17.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide whether to remove CEO Jensen Huang, and its shares fell about 6% before the market opened Thursday. CNBC confirmed the meeting after The Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to oust Huang; no decision had been announced by early Thursday. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a second extramarital relationship, with an Nvidia executive who reports to him; Huang admitted on Sunday to an affair with a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy, and the board opened an investigation. Nvidia's bylaws let a majority of its 11 directors remove the CEO. Shares were down 6.3% in premarket trading at 4:34 a.m. ET, after falling more than 8% after hours Wednesday; Bernstein cut its price target to $200 from $400.

Microsoft's Outlook, Teams and other 365 services went down for hours Thursday, with more than 130,000 Outlook problem reports at the peak. Downdetector logged more than 130,000 Outlook reports at 1:27 p.m. ET, Reuters reported. Microsoft said a large number of servers became unexpectedly unavailable after failing automated health checks, pushing load onto the rest of its systems; it paused all deployments and configuration changes and restarted servers. Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Defender XDR were listed as affected. As of about 4 p.m. ET Microsoft said a new health-check method was returning servers to service and was being applied more broadly, and that recent configuration updates were a potential cause still under investigation.

President Trump said the U.S. does not need a deal with Iran, days after saying talks to end the war were progressing; oil prices rose. "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday. On Sunday he had said new strikes were highly unlikely as talks progressed. Brent crude rose 1.9% to $94.48 a barrel and U.S. crude 2% to $88.19 during the day, CNBC reported; both had fallen sharply in November on hopes the war was ending.

Indonesia's Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigned after court rulings found his overseas high-school credentials fell short of legal requirements. Gibran, 39, the son of former President Joko Widodo, handed his resignation letter to the People's Consultative Assembly on Thursday, a day after 120 lawmakers began an impeachment push. President Prabowo Subianto said he accepted it "with a heavy heart." Gibran said the decision was personal and his documents were complete. The assembly must elect a replacement within 60 days from two candidates the president nominates. The rupiah hit a record low of 18,255 per dollar, Reuters reported.

A Justice Department-led crackdown on dark-web drug sellers, Operation TorNado, led to 354 arrests in 14 countries, officials said. DOJ said the operation by its Joint Criminal Opioid and Darknet Enforcement team, the largest in that team's history, seized 5.7 metric tons of drugs, 209 firearms and more than $234 million in cryptocurrency and cash. It targeted vendors who sold opioids, fentanyl and other drugs to tens of thousands of U.S. residents.

A gunman killed one person and wounded four at and near a Washington gym in Logan Circle, then fatally shot himself, police said. Interim D.C. police chief Jeffery Carroll said one person was killed inside VIDA Fitness at 15th and P streets NW and four others were injured, one seriously, some at a construction site across the street. The suspect died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound while barricaded in his apartment. Nearly a dozen nearby public schools locked down and residents sheltered in place until police gave the all-clear around 11:15 a.m.

item.title: Morning Edition, Thursday, November 12, 2026
item.description:
Democrat Scott Colom won Mississippi's U.S. Senate race, defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and becoming the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction. The AP called the race just before 6 p.m. ET Wednesday, after a Jackson County update put Colom ahead by 4,669 votes of 962,237 counted, about half a percentage point. Hyde-Smith conceded in a video: "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters." Mississippi has no recount law, and counties must certify results by Friday. The AP says the win gives Democrats 55 Senate seats in the new Congress, a net gain of eight. Alaska is the last uncalled Senate race.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide whether to remove CEO Jensen Huang, and its shares fell about 6% before the market opened Thursday. CNBC confirmed the meeting after The Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to oust Huang; no decision had been announced by early Thursday. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a second extramarital relationship, with an Nvidia executive who reports to him; Huang admitted on Sunday to an affair with a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy, and the board opened an investigation. Nvidia's bylaws let a majority of its 11 directors remove the CEO. Shares were down 6.3% in premarket trading at 4:34 a.m. ET, after falling more than 8% after hours Wednesday; Bernstein cut its price target to $200 from $400.

The SS United States, the 1952 ocean liner that still holds the transatlantic speed record, was sunk off Florida's Gulf Coast Wednesday to become the world's largest artificial reef. The 1,000-foot ship was scuttled without explosives in an hourslong operation about 20 nautical miles offshore between Destin-Fort Walton Beach and Pensacola. Okaloosa County bought it for about $1 million in 2024 and paid for the roughly $13 million reef project with tourist-tax revenue, after a year of cleanup in Mobile, Ala.

Saudi Arabia said debris from two intercepted ballistic missiles fell in the Mecca region, the latest in an escalating exchange of attacks with Yemen's Houthis. Saudi state TV said debris fell in the village of Sabouha, about 35 km northeast of Mecca's Grand Mosque, and in Wadi al-Maghamas, about 21 km east of it. The Saudi Civil Defence called it a "flagrant violation of international humanitarian law." The Houthis have denied targeting Mecca and Medina and had not commented.

U.S. stocks rose Wednesday as AI shares rebounded, with the S&P 500 up 1.3% and nearly back from last week's AI-driven sell-off. The Associated Press reported the S&P 500 rose 98.45 points to 7,619.38, within 2.6% of its October record. The Nasdaq rose 1.6% to 25,466.19 and the Dow rose 254.60 points, or 0.5%, to 52,486.49. CoreWeave led the gains after reporting stronger summer results than analysts expected. The bond market was closed for Veterans Day, and oil prices rose.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved from his Washington home to a U.S. military base after Iranian threats against his life, people familiar with the move told Reuters. The New York Times first reported the move; the base was not named. A Treasury spokesperson said Bessent "will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade." A source said concerns grew because a published aerial photo let his Georgetown home be located. The Times said at least a half dozen top officials have moved to bases or secure housing over the past year. Iran has previously denied plotting to attack officials on U.S. soil. The move follows Tuesday's federal indictment of three Iran-backed operatives over nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks in Europe and the U.S.

The White House's top lawyer warned incoming House Oversight chair Robert Garcia that Democrats' planned investigations of the administration "may cross the line into blatant criminality." In a three-page letter dated Monday, White House counsel Will Scharf wrote that congressional investigations need a "legitimate legislative purpose" and that "issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation." The letter announced no charges or probe. Garcia, a California Democrat expected to lead the committee when Democrats take the House in January, replied that "Congress' authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House."

President Trump used his Veterans Day speech at Arlington National Cemetery to defend the Iran war, saying it will end "soon" with "total victory." "America did not start a war with Iran. Iran has been waging war on America since 1979," Trump said after laying a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. "We want to make sure we have a total victory. Not a 93% victory." He said "we lost 18 beautiful souls"; Pentagon casualty figures list 23 U.S. service members killed and at least 865 wounded in connection with the war. He also said his planned triumphal arch near the cemetery would be dedicated "soon." On Tuesday, nine Kennedy family members asked a federal court to block the arch, saying it would shadow President John F. Kennedy's grave.

item.title: Morning Edition, Wednesday, November 11, 2026
item.description:
The resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was sent to the House Judiciary Committee on a 211-204 vote, blocking a floor vote on removing him. The House voted Tuesday at 6:02 p.m. ET on a motion to refer Rep. Thomas Massie's resolution (H. Res. 1655) to committee: 210 Republicans and one independent voted yes; 203 Democrats and Massie, a Kentucky Republican, voted no; 18 members did not vote (7 Republicans, 11 Democrats), the House Clerk's roll call shows. The articles accused Hegseth over his conduct in office and his handling of the Iran war. The committee is not required to act, and Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January.

Iran declared Argentina's navy and air force "terrorist organizations," in reply to Argentina's March listing of Iran's Revolutionary Guard. Iran's Foreign Ministry said it acted under a 2019 law allowing reciprocal steps against countries that back the U.S. designation of the Revolutionary Guard, and said Argentina would bear responsibility for the consequences; it named no specific measures. Argentina's government designated the Guard a terrorist group on March 31, citing the 1992 Israeli Embassy and 1994 AMIA bombings in Buenos Aires, which killed 29 and 85 people. Iran denies involvement.

Russia's Baltic oil port of Ust-Luga caught fire after a Ukrainian drone attack overnight, injuring three workers, the regional governor said. Leningrad region Governor Alexander Drozdenko said about 150 drones were shot down over the region and a transformer substation was shut down. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia warned of a drone threat, and Finland imposed temporary partial airspace and maritime curbs. In the Smolensk region, the governor said drone debris hit an apartment building in Yartsevo, killing two people. The strikes came as Russian and Ukrainian delegations began a second day of U.S.-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi.

A minivan crashed into people outside a Los Angeles Metro station in North Hollywood at rush hour Tuesday, killing three, authorities said. The vehicle ended up under a food vendor's tent at the busy Lankershim and Chandler boulevards intersection just before 6 p.m. local time. The driver, a man in his 60s, and at least two others were critically injured. Police have not given a cause.

Jim Jordan will lead House Republicans in the minority after beating Steve Scalise 106-73, while Senate Republicans kept John Thune as their leader. Jordan, the Ohio Republican who chairs the Judiciary Committee and co-founded the Freedom Caucus, won a secret-ballot vote of Republicans who will serve in the next Congress over Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana; Speaker Mike Johnson did not run. Tom Emmer of Minnesota beat August Pfluger of Texas for whip, the No. 2 minority post, and Lisa McClain of Michigan kept the conference chair job. In the Senate, Republicans first voted 31-15 to hold elections Tuesday rather than delay them, then re-elected Thune as leader, John Barrasso as whip and Tom Cotton as conference chair by acclamation. Both parties' leaders take their new minority roles when the new Congress convenes in January.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called the effort to impeach him "a farce" in his first Pentagon news conference in six months, hours before a scheduled House vote. Hegseth said the operations cited in Rep. Thomas Massie's eight articles, including the Iran war, strikes on suspected drug boats and actions in Venezuela and Yemen, were lawful orders from the commander in chief and called the charges "partisan policy disagreements." The House scheduled a procedural vote for about 5:30 p.m. ET Tuesday on whether to block or refer the resolution; if that fails, Massie said he will seek a separate vote on each article. Removal would require a House impeachment and a two-thirds Senate vote; retiring Sen. Thom Tillis said he is "likely to vote against Hegseth" if a trial comes.

Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, after 0.6% in September, the Labor Department said; prices excluding food and energy rose 0.3%. Shelter rose 0.3% and accounted for over 30% of the monthly increase; food rose 0.5% and energy 0.7%, with gasoline up 1.0%. Used cars and trucks and communication fell. Core prices rose 0.3% for a third straight month. BLS published no 12-month inflation rates because it collected no October 2025 data during the 2025 government shutdown. Separately, real average hourly earnings for all employees were unchanged from September, as hourly pay and prices both rose 0.4%.

Nvidia's independent directors hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon Kim and the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate CEO Jensen Huang, as the stock fell again. The board said the probe will examine whether company secrets or national security were compromised after Huang told staff he had an affair with a woman U.S. officials reportedly believe worked for Chinese intelligence; she has not been charged. Nvidia shares closed down about 5.5% Tuesday at $168.89 after a 4.3% drop Monday, and Reuters reported Microsoft briefly passed Nvidia as the world's second-most valuable company, the first time since June 2025. Reuters said it could not verify a report by The Information on the woman's role in chip sales to China.

Three Iran-backed operatives were charged in Manhattan with roles in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks in Europe and the U.S., including a plot against Britain's RAF Fairford. The eight-count superseding indictment unsealed Tuesday charges Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism offenses in support of Iran's Revolutionary Guard and Kata'ib Hizballah. Prosecutors allege al-Hassani orchestrated the September plot at RAF Fairford, which then housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel, and that al-Saadi, jailed in New York since his May arrest, passed coded messages through third parties to help coordinate it. Only al-Saadi is in custody. The charges are allegations.

A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile off Oman near the Strait of Hormuz, the British military's maritime agency UKMTO said; the crew is safe. UKMTO said the master of the tanker reported the hit at 1338 UTC (8:38 a.m. ET) Tuesday about 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman. No environmental damage was reported, and the master will assess damage at first light. The tanker was not named and UKMTO did not say who fired. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed further attacks that have not been independently confirmed.

The U.N. review of the U.S. human rights record was postponed to January after the Trump administration skipped it for a second time. The U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva agreed to move the Universal Periodic Review of the United States to Jan. 18-29, 2027, after Washington did not attend Tuesday's rescheduled session. Every U.N. member state goes through the review about every four to five years.

item.title: Morning Edition, Tuesday, November 10, 2026
item.description:
The Iran war is "militarily effectively over," President Trump said Monday after meeting Qatar's prime minister, adding that renewed U.S. strikes are "quite unlikely." In a surprise White House briefing-room appearance, Trump said, "Iran militarily is effectively over. We're just keeping it the status quo," and that Iran has been "decapitated," but he is still seeking a long-term solution to Iran's nuclear program. He said he saw "positive momentum" and a "good chance" the war could end, but "we're locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes." In a Truth Social post he said Gulf allies including Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE "would prefer the status quo." Trump gave no sign of a troop drawdown and said the naval blockade on Iranian oil continues: "We're keeping it going." Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, said they discussed "ways to progress the US-Iran talks." No deal has been announced.

U.S.-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine began Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, their first three-way meeting since February. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner lead the American side in the two-day talks; Ukraine's delegation is led by Rustem Umerov and Russia's by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky. Umerov said Kyiv's priorities are ending hostilities, reliable postwar security guarantees, economic recovery and humanitarian measures; Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said security issues would top the agenda. Moscow still demands Ukraine withdraw from four regions and abandon its NATO bid, which Kyiv rejects. Overnight, Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 162 drones and a ballistic missile.

A bipartisan bill to speed permits for power plants, transmission lines and other energy projects cleared its first Senate test vote Monday, 73-25. The Senate invoked cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 2347, the vehicle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, its first major action since the midterms; 51 Republicans, 21 Democrats and one independent voted yes. The 494-page bill, written by Sens. Martin Heinrich, Sheldon Whitehouse, Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee, would limit how long lawsuits and reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act can run, protect already issued permits, expand federal power to site big interstate transmission lines and make data-center developers pay for grid upgrades they need. President Trump backs it; some environmental groups and the National Congress of American Indians oppose it, and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he is still reviewing it. Debate resumes at noon Tuesday with roll-call votes expected; the bill still needs final Senate passage and House approval.

The FBI is looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese agent, President Trump said, adding Huang will be "in good shape." "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said at Monday's White House briefing, calling Huang "a very honorable man" and saying Huang told him he "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy." China's foreign ministry called the spy allegation "unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China." Huang has apologized for the affair and said he supports Nvidia's independent board investigation and will cooperate fully. Trump is due to meet Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen next week.

China's trade surplus topped $1 trillion for a second straight year, as October exports jumped 35% from a year earlier, customs data showed. China logged a $1.04 trillion surplus from January through October. October's surplus was $105.3 billion, down from $133.5 billion in September; imports also rose. Strong demand for high-tech goods such as computer chips and autos drove exports.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces a forced House impeachment vote after Rep. Thomas Massie filed eight articles Monday, mostly over the Iran war. Massie, a Kentucky Republican retiring at the end of the year, filed the resolution as privileged as the House returned Monday for its first session since the midterms, which requires House leaders to bring it to the floor within two legislative days, by Wednesday; Republicans can instead move to table it or refer it to committee by majority vote. Three articles charge waging the Iran war without a declaration, authorization or imminent threat, in violation of the War Powers Resolution; others cite ignoring civilian-casualty laws, the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific boat strikes, the capture of Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro without congressional approval, strikes on Yemen, and the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly. A simple House majority would impeach; removal would need two-thirds of the Senate.

Stocks had their best day since April Monday, with the S&P 500 up 2.3%, as oil prices fell and Nvidia sank on its CEO probe. The S&P 500 rose to 7,549.94, the Dow gained 1,104 points (2.2%) to 52,389.75 and the Nasdaq climbed 2.7% to 25,253.14, recovering most of last week's midterm-driven selloff in AI stocks. Brent crude fell more than 5% to about $92.60 a barrel on hopes for Iran diplomacy. Nvidia fell 4.3% after its board opened an independent investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Border wall construction in Texas's Big Bend region can resume after the Supreme Court paused a judge's order blocking it, 8-1. In an unsigned order in Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church, the court stayed U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone's Oct. 2 preliminary injunction while the case continues, saying the government is "exceedingly likely to prevail" that she lacked jurisdiction; the law lets courts hear only constitutional claims against the Homeland Security secretary's environmental-law waivers, and "there is no such thing as a 'constitutional' major-questions claim." The court cited border security and costs of nearly $500,000 a day from the halt. It declined to summarily reverse. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson would have denied the stay. This is not a final ruling on the waivers.

DACA recipients could get permanent legal status through a bipartisan deal, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, but "amnesty is never going to be a solution." Mullin told reporters Monday that President Trump encouraged him to work with Democrats who had reached out, that no concrete policy changes have been discussed yet, and that any DACA fix is up to Congress. His comments followed Trump's Sunday 60 Minutes interview saying the deportation crackdown "might be too tough" and a deal on long-term immigrants is "doable."

Brett Shumate, head of the Justice Department's Civil Division, resigned Monday, the fourth senior DOJ official to leave since the midterms, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced. Shumate follows Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon, National Security Division head John Eisenberg and Miami U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones. Blanche credited the Civil Division with suits against sanctuary policies, settlements over corporate DEI practices, and closing clinics that provided gender-affirming care to minors. It was not clear whether the administration will seek Senate-confirmed replacements before Republicans lose Senate control in January.
